text: The history of Kashmir is deeply connected to the broader history of the Indian subcontinent and has been influenced by Central and East Asia. Historically, Kashmir referred only to the Kashmir Valley in the western Himalayas; today, it encompasses the Indian-administered union territories of Jammu and Kashmir (including Jammu and the Kashmir Valley) and Ladakh, the Pakistan-administered territories of Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and the Chinese-administered regions of Aksai Chin and the Trans-Karakoram Tract. In the first half of the 1st millennium, the region was a center of Hinduism and later Buddhism under the Mauryas and Kushanas. During the ninth century, the Karkota Dynasty fostered a native Shaiva tradition that flourished for seven centuries under the Utpala and Lohara dynasties, ending in the mid-14th century. Islam began spreading in the 13th century, accelerated during the 14th and 15th centuries, and led to the decline of Kashmiri Shaivism. In 1339, Shah Mir became the first Muslim ruler, founding the Shah Mir dynasty. Muslim monarchs ruled Kashmir for five centuries, including the Mughal Empire from 1586 to 1751 and the Afghan Durrani Empire from 1747 to 1819. In 1819, the Sikhs, under Ranjit Singh, annexed Kashmir after defeating the Afghans. Following the Sikh defeat in the First Anglo-Sikh War in 1846, the Treaty of Lahore and the Treaty of Amritsar transferred control to the Raja of Jammu, Gulab Singh, who became the new ruler. His descendants ruled under British paramountcy until 1947, when the former princely state became a disputed territory administered by India, Pakistan, and China. The name "Kashmir" is etymologically derived from Sanskrit "ka" (water) and "shimīra" (desiccate), meaning "desiccated land," based on the legend that sage Kashyapa drained a lake in the valley at Baramulla, creating the settlement known as Kashyapa-pura, linked to ancient geographical references like Kaspapyros and Kaspatyros. The Nilamata Purana (c. 500–600 CE) records early history, though it is considered inconsistent; Kalhana's Rajatarangini, completed by 1150 CE, chronicles Kashmir's dynasties and is credited as India's first historian, relying on traditional sources and personal observations. During Muslim rule, three supplements to Rajatarangini were written by Jonaraja, Srivara, and Prajyabhatta and Suka, ending with Akbar's conquest in 1586. These were translated into Persian by scholars like Nizam Uddin, Farishta, and Abul Fazl. Key Persian texts include Baharistan-i-Shahi and Haidar Mailk's Tarikh-i-Kashmir (completed in 1621), both based on Rajatarangini and Persian histories. Archaeological findings at the Lower-Middle Palaeolithic Galander site near Pampore show remains of Palaeoloxodon turkmenicus and stone tools dating to 400–300,000 years ago, suggesting early human activity. Neolithic sites in the Kashmir Valley date to around 3000 BCE, with Burzahom showing two phases: the first (c. 2920 BCE) with mud-plastered pit dwellings and coarse pottery, and the second (until c. 1700 BCE) with ground-level houses and animal burials, including evidence of wheat, barley, and lentils. The megalithic phase featured massive circles and black burnished pottery. During the Vedic period, the Uttara–Kurus settled in Kashmir. In 326 BCE, Porus sought help from Abhisares, the king of Kashmir, against Alexander the Great, who later submitted after losing the Battle of Hydaspes. Under Ashoka (304–232 BCE), Kashmir became part of the Maurya Empire and Buddhism was introduced, with stupas, Shiva shrines, and Srinagari (Srinagar) built. Kanishka (127–151 CE) conquered Kashmir and founded Kanishkapur; Buddhist tradition holds he held the Fourth Buddhist Council there, with scholars like Ashvagosha, Nagarjuna, and Vasumitra participating. By the fourth century, Kashmir became a center of learning for both Buddhism and Hinduism, with missionaries spreading Buddhism to Tibet and China, and pilgrims visiting from these regions. Kumārajīva (343–413 CE) traveled to China, influencing Emperor Yao Xing and translating Sanskrit works. The Alchon Huns, under Toramana, conquered Kashmir, and Mihirakula (c. 502–530 CE) led campaigns across North India, defeating Yasodharman and destroying Buddhist shrines before retreating to Kashmir. After his defeat, he ruled there and committed atrocities. The Huns' influence faded after his death. In 659, Kashmir submitted to the Tang Dynasty's protectorate under Emperor Gaozong. Hindu dynasties ruled from the 7th to 14th centuries, with significant developments in Kashmiri Hinduism, including the rise of Kashmir Shaivism through scholars like Vasugupta (c. 875–925 CE) and Abhinavagupta (c. 975–1025 CE). The Karkota Empire (8th century) expanded under Chandrapida and Lalitaditya Muktapida, who defeated Tibetans, Yashovarman of Kanyakubja, and kingdoms in Magadha, Kamarupa, Gauda, and Kalinga, extending influence to Malwa and Gujarat and defeating Arabs at Sindh; the dynasty ended around 855–856 CE. The Utpala dynasty, founded by Avantivarman, was followed by Shankaravarman (885–902 CE), who fought the Gurjaras. Political instability in the 10th century led to the rise of the Tantrins, causing chaos until defeated by Chakravarman. Queen Didda, of Hindu Shahi descent, ruled in the second half of the 10th century. After her death in 1003 CE, the Lohara dynasty took over. Suhadeva, the last Lohara king, fled after a raid by Zulju (Dulacha), a Turkic–Mongol chief, around 1320; his wife, Queen Kota Rani, ruled until 1339 and is credited with building the "Kutte Kol" canal to divert Jhelum waters. Mahmud of Ghazni attempted to conquer Kashmir in the 11th century but failed due to the fortress at Lohkot. Historian Mohibbul Hasan argues that oppressive taxation, corruption, and the rise of feudal lords during the Lohara dynasty (1003–1320 CE) enabled foreign invasions. Rinchana, a Tibetan Buddhist refugee, ruled after Zulju; folklore suggests he converted to Islam due to political pressure from his minister Shah Mir, who then led a coup to establish Muslim rule. In the 14th century, Islam became dominant in Kashmir. Islamic preacher Sheikh Nooruddin Noorani (Nund Rishi) combined Kashmir Shaivism with Sufism. Sultans from 1354 to 1470 were generally tolerant, except Sultan Sikandar (1389–1413), who imposed taxes, forced conversions, and earned the title But–Shikan for destroying idols. Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (c. 1420–1470) invited artists from Central Asia and Persia, leading to prosperity in wood carving, papier-mâché, shawls, and carpets. In the 1470s, states of Jammu, Poonch, and Rajauri revolted against Sultan Hajji Khan but were subdued by his son Hasan Khan in 1472. By the mid-16th century, Hindu influence declined as Muslim missionaries from Central Asia and Persia arrived, and Persian replaced Sanskrit as the official language. The Chak nobility eventually unseated the Shah Mir dynasty. Mughal general Haidar Dughlat invaded Kashmir in c. 1540 on behalf of Humayun, but was overthrown due to persecution of Shias, Shafi'is, and Sufis and revolts. Kashmir came under direct Mughal rule in 1586 under Akbar, who added it to the Kabul Subah; Shah Jahan later carved it into a separate subah with its seat in Srinagar. Gardens, mosques, and palaces were built under successive Mughal rulers, but religious intolerance and discriminatory taxes returned under Aurangzeb in 1658. After his death, Mughal influence declined. In 1700, a Kashmiri merchant's servant brought Mo-i Muqqadas (the Prophet's hair) to the valley, which was housed in the Hazratbal Shrine. Nadir Shah's invasion in 1738 weakened Mughal control. The Afghan Durrani Empire took control in 1752; the governor Sukh Jiwan Mal rebelled in the mid-1750s but was defeated in 1762. The Durrani rulers oppressed the Hindu population through forced conversions, killings, and forced labor, with a heavy tax burden; historian Victoria Schofield notes the cruelty was mainly directed at Hindus, and many Kashmiris were sold into slavery. The Durrani Empire controlled Kashmir until 1819, after which it was annexed by the Sikh Empire. After the Battle of Shopian in 1819, the Sikhs took control. Initially welcomed due to suffering under the Afghans, Sikh rule proved oppressive, with anti-Muslim laws such as death sentences for cow slaughter, closure of the Jamia Masjid in Srinagar, and banning the azaan, though these were later repealed by governor Muhyuddin. European visitors noted the poverty of the Muslim peasantry and exorbitant taxes under Sikh rule.

The empire controlled Kashmir until 1819, after which the region was annexed by the Sikh Empire. After four centuries of Muslim rule, Kashmir fell to the Sikhs under Ranjit Singh of Punjab following the Battle of Shopian in 1819. The Kashmiris, having suffered under the Afghans, initially welcomed the Sikh rulers, but Sikh governors proved to be hard taskmasters, and Sikh rule was generally considered oppressive, possibly due to the region's remoteness from the Sikh capital in Lahore. The Sikhs enacted anti-Muslim laws, including death sentences for cow slaughter, closing the Jamia Masjid in Srinagar, and banning the azaan, though these laws were later repealed by governor Muhyuddin in the final decade of Sikh rule. European visitors noted the abject poverty of the Muslim peasantry and exorbitant taxes under the Sikhs, with high taxes reportedly depopulating large areas and leaving only one-sixteenth of cultivable land under cultivation. After the 1832 famine, the Sikhs reduced land tax to half the produce and began offering interest-free loans, making Kashmir the second highest revenue earner for the Sikh Empire. During this period, Kashmiri shawls gained global recognition, especially in the West. In 1780, after Ranjit Deo's death, the Sikh Empire captured the kingdom of Jammu and made it a tributary. Ranjit Deo's grandnephew, Gulab Singh, served at Ranjit Singh’s court, distinguished himself in military campaigns, and was appointed Raja of Jammu in 1820. With officer Zorawar Singh, Gulab Singh captured Ladakh and Baltistan for the Sikhs. Notable Sikh governors of Kashmir included Moti Ram, Hari Singh, Kirpa Ram, Mihan Singh, and Muhyuddin. In 1845, the First Anglo-Sikh War began, and Gulab Singh remained neutral until the Battle of Sobraon in 1846, when he acted as a mediator and trusted advisor to Sir Henry Lawrence. Two treaties were signed: the first saw the British receive the hill countries between Beas and Indus in exchange for ten million rupees; the second transferred to Gulab Singh, for seven point five million rupees, all mountainous territory east of the Indus and west of the Ravi (i.e., the Vale of Kashmir). The Treaty of Amritsar freed Gulab Singh from Sikh obligations and made him Maharajah of Jammu and Kashmir. The Dogras' loyalty proved valuable during the 1857 revolt, as they refused to shelter mutineers, allowed English women and children to seek asylum in Kashmir, and sent troops to fight for the British, leading the British to secure Dogra succession. After Gulab Singh's death in 1857, his son Ranbir Singh added the emirates of Hunza, Gilgit, and Nagar to the kingdom. The Princely State of Kashmir and Jammu (1820–1858) was artificial in composition and lacked a coherent identity due to its disparate origins and autocratic rule. It combined diverse regions, religions, and ethnicities: eastern Ladakh was ethnically and culturally Tibetan with Buddhist inhabitants; southern Jammu had a mixed Hindu, Muslim, and Sikh population; the central Kashmir Valley was predominantly Sunni Muslim with a small but influential Hindu minority (Kashmiri pandits); northeast Baltistan had a population ethnically related to Ladakh but practicing Shi'a Islam; northern Gilgit Agency had diverse, mostly Shi'a groups; and western Punch was Muslim but of a different ethnicity. Despite being a majority, Muslims faced severe oppression under Hindu rule through high taxes, forced labor, and discriminatory laws. Many Kashmiri Muslims migrated from the Valley to Punjab due to famine and Dogra policies. The Muslim peasantry was vast, impoverished, lacked education and political awareness, and was chronically in debt to landlords and moneylenders, organizing politically only in the 1930s. Ranbir Singh's grandson Hari Singh, who became ruler in 1925, was the monarch in 1947 at the time of British withdrawal and the partition of British India into India and Pakistan. An internal revolt began in Poonch against oppressive taxation, and in August, Maharaja’s forces fired upon pro-Pakistan demonstrations, burned villages, and massacred civilians. The Poonch rebels declared an independent "Azad" Kashmir on 24 October. Rulers were encouraged to accede to either India or Pakistan, considering geographical contiguity and people's wishes. In 1947, Jammu and Kashmir’s population was 77% Muslim and 20% Hindu. To delay a decision, the Maharaja signed a standstill agreement with Pakistan, pending with India. In October 1947, Pashtun tribesmen from Pakistan’s North-West Frontier Province, recruited by Poonch rebels and incensed by atrocities, invaded Kashmir, engaging in looting and killing. The rebels’ goal was to intimidate Hari Singh into submission. Instead, the Maharaja appealed to the British, who agreed on the condition that he accede to India. After signing the Instrument of Accession, Indian troops entered Kashmir and expelled the Pakistani-sponsored irregulars from most of the state. India accepted the accession as provisional until the will of the people could be determined. Sheikh Abdullah endorsed the accession as temporary and was appointed head of the emergency administration. Pakistan immediately contested the accession, claiming it was fraudulent, that the Maharaja acted under duress, and that he had not terminated the standstill agreement with Pakistan. In early 1948, India sought a UN resolution on the Kashmir conflict. The United Nations Commission for India and Pakistan (UNCIP) was established, and the UN Security Council passed Resolution 47 on 21 April 1948, insisting that the people of J&K determine their accession through a free and impartial plebiscite. The Indian Prime Minister urged the UN to conduct a referendum on the results. However, India insisted no referendum could occur until all irregulars were cleared. On 5 January 1949, UNCIP stated that the accession of J&K to India or Pakistan would be decided by a plebiscite. Both countries accepted the principle that Pakistan withdraw its intruders and Indian forces, followed by a truce and plebiscite, but failed to reach a truce due to disagreements on demilitarization—specifically whether the Azad Kashmiri army should be disbanded during the truce or plebiscite phase. A ceasefire was agreed in late 1948 under UN auspices, but the plebiscite was never held, leading to deteriorating India-Pakistan relations and three subsequent wars in 1965, 1971, and 1999. India controls about half of the former princely state, Pakistan controls a third, governing it as Gilgit–Baltistan and Azad Kashmir. According to Encyclopædia Britannica, despite a clear Muslim majority in Kashmir before 1947 and its geographic and cultural ties to Muslim-majority Punjab, the region was divided. Pakistan ended up with thinly populated, inaccessible, and underdeveloped territory, while the largest Muslim group in the Valley—over half the region’s population—remained in Indian-administered territory, with its access to the Jhelum valley route blocked. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 39 in January 1948 to establish a special commission to investigate the conflict. Following the commission’s recommendations, Resolution 47 (21 April 1948) required the withdrawal of Pakistani forces from J&K and a plebiscite to determine accession, supervised by the UN. Subsequent resolutions noted India’s failure to hold the plebiscite, but no punitive action could be taken because the resolution was non-binding. Pakistan never withdrew its forces and retained occupation. The eastern region of the former princely state has faced a boundary dispute. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, boundary agreements between Britain, Afghanistan, and Russia over northern Kashmir were signed, but China never accepted them, and its position remained unchanged after the 1949 communist revolution. By the mid-1950s, the Chinese army entered northeastern Ladakh, completed a military road through Aksai Chin by 1956–57 to connect Xinjiang and western Tibet, and India’s discovery of this road led to border clashes culminating in the Sino-Indian War of October 1962. China has occupied Aksai Chin since 1962 and also acquired the Trans-Karakoram Tract from Pakistan in 1965. In 1949, the Indian government compelled Hari Singh to step down and transfer power to Sheikh Abdullah, leader of the National Conference Party. Since then, India and Pakistan have remained in bitter enmity, with three wars over Kashmir, and the growing dispute and democratic failure have fueled Kashmiri nationalism and militancy. In 1986, the Anantnag riots erupted after CM Gul Shah ordered the construction of a mosque at a Hindu temple in Jammu and made an incendiary speech. Hindu-Muslim riots, triggered by the opening of Babri Masjid to Hindu worshippers, spread to seven other states. Following the 1987 Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly election, widely seen as rigged, disgruntled youth such as the 'HAJY group'—Abdul Hamid Shaikh, Ashfaq Majid Wani, Javed Ahmed Mir, and Mohammed Yasin Malik—joined the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF) as an alternative to the ineffective democratic system. This intensified the insurgency in the Valley. In 1989, conflict intensified as Mujahideen from Afghanistan infiltrated the region after the Soviet–Afghan War ended. Pakistan provided arms and training to both indigenous and foreign militants, worsening discontent. In August 2019, the Indian government repealed the special status granted to Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 of the Indian Constitution and passed the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, dissolving the state and reorganizing it into two union territories: Jammu and Kashmir (west) and Ladakh (east), effective from 31 October 2019. In the 1901 British Indian Empire Census, the princely state of Kashmir had a population of 2,905,578: 2,154,695 Muslims, 689,073 Hindus, 25,828 Sikhs, and 35,047 Buddhists. Hindus were mainly in Jammu, where they made up just under 50% of the population. In the Kashmir Valley, Hindus numbered only 524 per 10,000 (5.24%), and in Ladhakh and Gilgit only 94 per 10,000 (0.94%). The total Valley population was 1,157,394, of which 1,083,766 (93.6%) were Muslims. These percentages have remained stable for over a century. In the 1941 British India Census, Muslims accounted for 93.6% of the Valley population and Hindus for 4%. In 2003, Muslims in the Valley were 95% and Hindus 4%; in Jammu, Hindus were 67% and Muslims 27%. Among Kashmiri Muslims, four divisions were recorded: Shaikhs, Saiyids, Mughals, and Pathans. The Shaikhs, the most numerous, are descendants of Hindus who abandoned caste rules and have clan names such as Tantre, Shaikh, Bat, Mantu, Ganai, Dar, Damar, Lon. Saiyids are divided into religious practitioners and those in agriculture; their kram name is 'Mir,' used as a prefix for religious ones and as an affix for agricultural ones. Mughals, though few, have kram names like Mir, Beg, Bandi, Bach, Ashaye. Pathans, more numerous than Mughals, are mainly in the southwest, with notable colonies like Kuki-Khel Afridis at Dranghaihama, retaining old customs and speaking Pashtu. Major Muslim tribes include Butts, Dar, Lone, Jat, Gujjar, Rajput, Sudhan, and Khatri. Some Butts, Dars, and Lones use the title Khawaja; Khatri use Shaikh; Gujjars use Chaudhary. All these tribes are indigenous to the region and converted from Hinduism to Islam. Among Jammu’s Hindus, who numbered 626,177, the details of their distribution are not fully provided in the text.

The Mughals, who were not numerous, used kram names such as "Mir" (a corruption of "Mirza"), "Beg", "Bandi", "Bach", and "Ashaye". The Pathans, who are more numerous than the Mughals, are primarily found in the south-west of the valley, where Pathan colonies have been established over time; the most notable is the Kuki-Khel Afridis at Dranghaihama, who maintain traditional customs and speak Pashtu. The main Muslim tribes in the princely state include the Butts, Dar, Lone, Jat, Gujjar, Rajput, Sudhan, and Khatri. A small number of Butts, Dar, and Lone use the title Khawaja, while the Khatri use the title Shaikh and the Gujjar use the title Chaudhary. All these tribes are indigenous to the princely state and converted to Islam from Hinduism upon their arrival in the region. Among the Hindus of Jammu province, who numbered 626,177 (or 90.87% of the Hindu population of the princely state), the major castes recorded in the census were Brahmins (186,000), Rajputs (167,000), Khatris (48,000), and Thakkars (93,000).
